solution.name: Cart abandonment
solution.metaTitle: Cart abandonment — and how recovery works
solution.metaDescription: Where the drop-off happens, why the checkout step is different from browsing, and how an automatic recovery sequence turns it back into orders.
solution.lede: Cart abandonment is the gap between the customers who reached the payment step and the customers who finished it. Understanding where that gap opens is what makes recovery possible at all.

sections.h: Abandonment is not the same as browsing
p: A visitor who leaves a product page never committed to anything. A visitor who reached checkout did: they chose the items, moved to payment, and stopped there. Those two people need different follow-ups, and only the second one is who recovery is for.
That distinction is why a recovery message can be specific — it can name the items, the total and the return link — while still not being a marketing message to a cold list.

sections.h: Why customers stop at the payment step
p: The reasons cluster into a few recurring shapes: an interruption (a call, a locked card, a distracted minute), a decision that needs more time than the moment allowed, an unexpected cost at the final screen, or a payment method that failed quietly.
Only some of those are worth chasing. An interruption is recovered by a reminder. A genuinely lost buyer is not recovered by a third email — that is why short sequences outperform long ones.
A recovery setup has three moving parts: detect the abandoned checkout, send a message on a schedule, and attribute the order that comes back so the sequence can be judged.
bullets: Detection — the abandoned checkout is captured as it happens
Timing — a first message around 1 hour, a follow-up around 24 hours
Channel — email by default, an optional single text where it fits
Attribution — recovered orders and revenue reported per store

p: Recovery works best on customers who were already close — it brings back a decision that was nearly made. A checkout that is slow or untrustworthy still has to be fixed at the source, and consent and sender registration stay with the store and its provider.

The Free plan covers the whole mechanics — both recovery channels and the timed sequence — up to its monthly limits. Store owners can judge whether recovery works for their catalog before paying for it.

faq.q: Is an abandoned cart the same as an abandoned checkout?
faq.a: For recovery purposes the checkout is what matters: it is the point where the customer committed to buying and where a reminder can still name the exact items and total.

faq.q: Can a recovery sequence send too much?
faq.a: It can, which is why the default here is two emails, not five — and why there is exactly one text per checkout when the SMS channel is on.

faq.q: Does recovery report back what it earned?
faq.a: Yes. Recovered orders and recovered revenue are reported per store, so the sequence can be assessed against orders rather than opens.
